review_text: Embodying the holy he-man Rama is Ranbir Kapoor, terrific in a role that requires stillness and integrity as much as it does action-hero authenticity.
A soulless, beat-for-beat execution that operates less as a bold cinematic adventure and more as a sanitised spectacle, akin to Jon Favreau’s live-action The Lion King remake.
While this Hindi action epic doesn't explore all the source material's complexities, this first of two parts shifts the spotlight away from hero Rama.
Undeniably exciting, most of all for Yash's carnal and venomous Ravana, and for the vibrant worlds it builds.
Every frame is wonderfully grandiose, bursting with sensuous physicality and opulence.
Ramayana: Part 1 may not go down as the best epic of the year, or even the best film of the year, but it is still a cinematic achievement that the Gods would approve of.
Yash gives it thunder; the visuals give it grandeur. What it needs is greater trust that the audience can recognise a moment’s importance without being made to linger over it.
A tremendously expensive, disappointingly safe update on a story the DNA of which can be found everywhere, and, therefore, there's not a lot more that Tiwari has to say.
Ramayana: Part 1 is a visual beast of epic proportion — ambitious, uneven, but one gamble that entirely rides on its scale, the much-touted 4000 crore budget.

A monumental cinematic experience! Nitesh Tiwari delivers breathtaking spectacle, thrilling action, and a commanding Yash as Ravana. Uneven pacing and abrupt time jumps lessen the emotional impact, but my appreciation only grew days after experiencing it.
Regardless of how you view the movie, one thing is certain: you MUST go see Namit Malhotra's Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.
A technical masterpiece, dragged down by Part One problems.

Three hours is a big time commitment for a story with a ton of characters to keep sorted, and if you’re not already versed in the mythology, only after Part 2 will we know for sure if it’s worth the investment.
[Nitesh] Tiwari does a remarkable job of keeping this gigantic, episodic story from ever feeling dull, and what’s more, he does it without leaving the adrenaline firehose spewing at full blast.

It would have been a far stronger film had it been as interested in exploring the emotional complexities of its characters as it is in showcasing their extraordinary powers. Even with that shortcoming, it's an experience one shouldn't miss.
It's not the epic triumph I was promised but it still has enough interesting set pieces, spectacle and narrative to carry it to the credits.
There’s something uniquely disorienting about watching a ton of money thrown at movie screens without any proportionate human warmth or craftsmanship.
